source.title: Angular Steering: Behavior Control via Rotation in Activation Space

record.file_problem: none; full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper applies directional ablation using a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means feature direction and reports refusal-related outcomes on new instruct models. It is a direct test of the ablation component of V1, though its direction selection and activation setup differ in some respects.
record.gate_note: Appendix C, Table 2 reports directional-ablation results against a no-steering baseline. Other angular-steering results use a rotation in a two-dimensional plane, not the claim's single-direction addition or removal, so they are not included as rows for V1. The paper's general-capability evaluations concern its angular-steering method, not the ablation results.
record.test_reason: Appendix C Table 2 reports directional ablation of a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction against no steering, on six instruct models and 104 held-out AdvBench prompts. The recipe differs from the original: ablation is applied to normalized activations after each RMSNorm, and the direction is chosen automatically by maximum mean cosine similarity. It is a different method aimed at V1's ablation question. The ablation is a baseline in a comparison of methods, but its no-steering contrast bears directly on V1.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors conclude that (Adaptive) Angular Steering gives continuous refusal control across six models while preserving benchmark accuracy and coherence. They report it matches or beats addition and ablation in Table 2. They also argue from perplexity that alignment masks rather than removes harmful behavior.
record.recipe_differences: The ablation comparison uses a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction and evaluates refusal-related metrics, but the paper selects directions automatically, extracts normalized activations, and does not establish that ablation is applied at every position as specified in V1.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model: the refusal-substring ablation score drops on the three Qwen models, is unchanged on the Llama models, and rises slightly on Gemma. The paper also reports that its angular-steering outcome depends on the steering plane and that smaller models are more vulnerable to interference.

fits_no_version.finding: Rotating normalized activations in a fixed plane spanned by the diff-in-means direction and the first PC of the per-layer candidates moves all six models continuously from refusal to compliance and back. A plane of two random directions has little to no effect in 5 of 6 models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A 2D plane containing the diff-in-means refusal direction gives continuous, bidirectional control of refusal; random planes do not.

record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the Table 2 ablation results. Refusal-substring matching detects phrases rather than refusal semantics, and the authors note that it does not assess coherence or harmfulness. The capability and perplexity checks concern angular steering, not the ablation operation assessed here. Table 2 also marks HarmBench and LLAMAGUARD with upward arrows, but the text does not make clear how those arrow directions correspond to the V1 prediction.
record.rows_left_out: No additional ablation results bearing on V1 were left out. Angular-steering results and random-plane experiments were not included as V1 rows because they intervene through a rotation plane rather than testing the single-direction ablation prediction.

untested.parts: Untested parts: adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts; ablation of raw residual-stream activations at every position, as in the original; capability retention under ablation specifically (the capability checks cover angular steering only).

missing.what: The Activation Addition baseline (presumably negative addition along the direction) reaches HarmBench 0.63–0.88, LlamaGuard about 0.98–0.99 and substring 0 on all six models, including those where ablation fails. This bears on whether the single direction mediates refusal.
A random-plane control shows little to no steering effect in 5 of 6 models. A plane of the feature direction plus one random direction degrades control except in Qwen2.5-7B.

record.verdict_notes: The cannot_determine states on the HarmBench and LlamaGuard rows were unjustified. Table 2's up-arrows mark harmful output as desired, consistent with AAS scores near 1, so higher means less refusal. Ablation here differs from the original in three ways: it is applied after each RMSNorm to normalized activations, the direction is auto-selected, and it is a baseline in a methods comparison. The weak ablation results may therefore reflect the recipe rather than the claim. Results are single runs with no uncertainty reported, n=104.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests directional ablation on harmful prompts, but does not test whether adding the direction induces refusal on harmless requests, whether ablation at every position removes all refusals, or whether general abilities remain intact specifically under ablation.
No weight-edit conversion or released-model abliteration is tested.
The paper does not test whether attacks suppress the direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
The paper's two-dimensional steering plane and random-plane ablation do not test whether refusal is better described by an affine set, cone, or multiple directions.
No separate harmfulness-judgment and refusal-decision representations are tested.
Directions are extracted separately for the tested models; cross-language or cross-model transfer of a direction is not tested.
The paper does not vary refusal-training data, timing, or procedure.
Reasoning models are not tested as target systems.

relation.reason: Appendix C Table 2 reports ablation against no steering on six models with refusal and harmful scores, so its own results bear on V1.

tranche.reason: Diff-in-means direction ablated at all layers and scored by substring plus guard classifiers, close to the original. But the direction is extracted from post-RMSNorm activations and picked automatically by cosine similarity (Remark 1), and the eval set is 104 AdvBench prompts. A different-recipe test fits T2.

source_check.notes: The text never states where Table 2's ablation is applied (it says only all layers, within Span(h, d_feat), 'as in [1, 50]'). Only direction extraction is stated as post-norm. Llama-3.1-8B ablation equals no steering exactly on all three measures, which may point to a no-op. Ablation was not tuned, unlike AAS and Addition. Missing from the rows: Fig. 9a shows near-baseline TinyBenchmarks performance near 90° in Span(h, d_feat), roughly ablation (figure only). Table 2's layout is lost in extraction, but its 24 blocks of three map without ambiguity.

statements.correction: Llama-3.2-3B substring 0.7885→0.7885; Llama-3.1-8B HarmBench 0.0577→0.0577, LlamaGuard 3 0.0385→0.0385, substring 0.9231→0.9231; Gemma-2-9B flat (substring 0.9904→1.0000). Qwen2.5-14B: substring 0.9808→0.0962 but HarmBench 0.0192→0.0288. Table 2 ablation runs at all layers in Span(h, d_feat), using an auto-selected direction from post-norm activations.
statements.problem: All numbers for this study are right. But Qwen2.5-14B is listed as weak ablation on HarmBench alone, though its refusal-substring score fell 0.9808→0.0962. For Qwen-14B the ablation removed refusal phrases and only harmful compliance stayed flat. That is measure dependence (the record's limits_scope group), not absent ablation. Also, the text never says outright that Table 2 ablation acts on normalized activations; only direction extraction is stated as post-norm.
